evidence.readmeExcerpt: # dsh-pilot ## 让 DSH 看见并高效地操作你的电脑 **Give DeepSeek Harness hands and eyes on your desktop.** [![awesome · DSH plugin](https://awesome-dsh-plugin.com/badge.svg)](https://awesome-dsh-plugin.com/p/momasiku/dsh-pilot/) [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@momasiku/dsh-pilot?label=npm)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@momasiku/dsh-pilot) [![compat](https://github.com/momasiku/dsh-pilot/actions/workflows/compat.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/momasiku/dsh-pilot/actions/workflows/compat.yml) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ![platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-0078d4.svg) [English](#why-this-exists) · [中文说明](#中文说明) > **Windows desktop control.** The model sees the real screen and drives the real > mouse and keyboard. Out of the box, a DeepSeek Harness session can reason about your desktop but cannot touch it: you describe what is on screen, you take the screenshots, you do the clicking, and you report what happened. **dsh-pilot closes that loop.** The model looks at the real pixels and then operates them: | tool | what it does | | --- | --- | | **`screen_view`** | captures the live desktop and returns the PNG as a **real image block** the model can see — not OCR, not a text summary | | **`desktop_control`** | moves the pointer, clicks, drags, scrolls, types, sends keys, focuses and lists windows — and can capture the result in the same call | | **`desktop_sequence`** | runs a **whole batch** of those actions in one call and looks once at the end | ```text You : 把浏览器里那个报表的第三列改名成 "Q3 收入"，然后保存 DSH : desktop_sequence([focus "报表.xlsx", click 812,430, type "Q3 收入", key enter, key ctrl+s]) → 1 round trip, 1 screenshot, per-step timings, done ``` ## Why this exists A model that cannot see the screen has to be told what is on it. A model that cannot touch the screen has to be told what to do next. That turns every desktop task into a conversation about the desktop instead of work on the desktop — and the user becomes the hands, the eyes, and the error message. The expensive part of desktop automation was never the mouse. It is **how many times the model and the computer have to talk**: | a five-step task: focus a window, click a field, type, press Enter, look at the result | DSH alone | DSH + dsh-pilot | | --- | --- | --- | | who reads the screen | you | the model, from real pixels | | who clicks and types | you | the model | | model ↔ computer round trips | 5 (one per step, plus yours) | **1** | | screenshots shipped to the model | 4–5 | **1** | | where the model spends its time | waiting, re-describing, re-asking | thinking about the task | | when a step fails | you notice | the same result says which step, and why | ## What it feels like ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as You participant M as Model participant P as dsh-pilot participant W as Warm worker (PowerShell) participant D as Your desktop U->>M: 把第三列改名成 Q3 收入并保存 M->>P: screen_view(window: "报表") P->>D: capture (per-monitor DPI aware) D-->>M: real PNG + cursor, foreground window, monitor bounds M->>P: desktop_sequence([focus, click, type, key, key]) P->>W: 5 requests over one pipe — 6–12 ms each W->>D: SetCursorPos, SendInput, clipboard paste D-->>M: one end frame (with coordinate rulers) + per-step outcome ``` ## Why the coordinates can be trusted The classic way a vision-driven click goes wrong is a coordinate that is *almost* right. dsh-pilot removes the three ways that happens: **1. Both halves are per-monitor DPI aware.** A DPI-unaware process is lied to by Windows: it sees a 2560×1600 panel as 1707×1067, so every click computed from such a screenshot lands in the wrong place. The sensor and the effector each declare `SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext(PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2)` before doing anything, so one image pixel is one physical screen pixel. **2. Frames carry rulers.** Ticks every 200 px along the top and left edge, each labelled with the **screen coordinate** it sits at, plus an `origin x,y step n` note. The model reads a position off the image instead of counting pixels — and because the labels are screen coordinates, they survive any downscaling the attachment store does. **3. The envelope says what it actually delivered.** If the store re-encodes a frame smaller, the model is told the ratio and the multiplier, and the coordinate contract becomes conditional — it only promises "use x and y as they are" when the delivered frame *is* the capture: ```text 1974x873 delivered 1974x873 = 0.873x capture; multiply image readings by 1.1454 to get screen pixels ``` ## Why it is fast Batching is the big win (round trips, not clicks). The second win is that PowerShell stops being restarted: one warm worker process answers every action and every frame. | request | one-shot script | warm worker | | --- | --- | --- | | action (`move`, `click`, `type`, …) | ~0.9–2.0 s | **6–12 ms** | | capture (primary monitor) | ~1.2–2.3 s | **~0.5 s** | Measured on a 2560×1600 panel at 150% scaling with the harness UI animating. The worker is started in the background on the first tool call, so the ~1 s it needs overlaps the first capture instead of delaying the first action. **Identical frames are not resent.** Every capture returns a `frameHash`; when a frame is byte-identical to the previous one of the same session, the image is not attached (or stored) again — the result says `unchanged: true` and the coordinates from the frame the model already has still apply. `forceImage: true` overrides it. ## Reading the control tree A screenshot costs a guess: the model finds a button in pixels, estimates its centre, clicks, and takes another frame to see whether the guess was right. Windows exposes the same control through UI Automation as a role, a name and a rectangle, so the click becomes the centre of that rectangle and nothing has to be looked at. ```js desktop_control({ action: 'controls', title: 'Notepad' }) // 4 [Button] '最小化' @ 887,1 45x39 // 14 [Button] '新建会话' @ 12,54 256x24 // 23 [Edit] '搜索会话名称' @ 204,238 4x20 offscreen desktop_control({ action: 'click', target: 14, title: 'Notepad' }) ``` **The tree is not a faster screenshot; it is a different trade.** | | screenshot | control tree | | --- | --- | --- | | one read | ~150 ms, ~1k tokens | ~130-300 ms, ~850 tokens (filtered) | | click target | estimated from pixels | the control's exact rectangle | | state | "looks disabled" | `enabled`, `offscreen`, `HasKeyboardFocus`, `IsSelected`, value | | availability | always | **not always** - see below | Per call the tree is slower or level. Per task it is much faster, because one read resolves several targets without another frame and without another round trip. **It does not always exist.** A canvas, a drawing surface, a custom-painted list and an Electron window that publishes nothing all give an empty or useless tree. That is why the screenshot path is still there and still the fallback: read the tree first, take a frame when the tree is empty or when you need to see what is drawn rather than what is declared. **Three things worth knowing.** - An index addresses one row of one listing. It is resolved against a fresh read at click time, and the worker remembers the listing it handed out, so a row that changed identity fails loudly instead of being clicked by position: `the control at index 4 is not the one that was listed: expected [Button] 'OK', found [Button] 'Cancel'`. - `meaningfulOnly` (default `true`) returns only the roles a person can operate. On a real 673-element window that is 77 elements and ~850 tokens instead of 9k - the rest is layout panes with no name, no state and nothing to click. Pass `false` for the whole tree. - `includeValues` is off by default: structure is not content. Password fields are masked even when it is on. **When the thing you want has no tree of its own** - a chat transcript, a canvas, a custom-painted panel - do not look for it. Look for what surrounds it and subtract: the composer is an `Edit` with a rectangle, the window has a rectangle, so the transcript is what is left between them. Or skip the geometry: select the item in the tree, confirm with `HasKeyboardFocus` that the keyboard is where you want it, type, press Enter. That last step is something a screenshot cannot do - it can show a caret, not a promise. ## Why it is safe Giving a model hands is the part worth getting right: - **Risk is declared, then enforced.** Low risk (default) batches freely. A batch declared `medium`/`high`, or one carrying a step marked `risk: "high"`, is refused *before anything touches the desktop* unless the caller passes `confirm: true` — which it does only after you agreed. - **`dryRun: true`** validates a batch and lists the plan without executing. - **Stop on the first failure** (default): a refused `focus` can never be followed by typing into whatever window happens to be in front. - **Targeted input.** When a step names a window (`hwnd`), the effector re-asserts it as foreground immediately before injecting, so a click cannot land in a neighbour. - **An unknown outcome is never a silent retry.** If the worker dies after a request was delivered, the action is reported as failed rather than repeated — it may already have taken effect. A capture has no side effects, so it *is* retried. - **Interruption works.** Pressing Esc writes a cancel token, the action loop polls it between every step (during drags, during the settle wait, before the capture) and a drag releases the button in a `finally` block, so an aborted turn cannot leave the mouse latched down or the remaining clicks playing out. - **It cannot lie about privilege.** Windows refuses input injection into a higher-integrity (elevated) window; the tool reports that failure instead of pretending it worked. - **`desktop_sequence` is bounded** by `maxSequenceSteps` (default 24). ## Install ```powershell # from npm (recommended) dsh plugin --profile add @momasiku/dsh-pilot # or from the repository dsh plugin --profile add github:momasiku/dsh-pilot # or this repository's prebuilt tarball, which skips the build-approval step dsh plugin --profile add https://github.com/momasiku/dsh-pilot/releases/latest/download/dsh-pilot.tgz # or a checkout you already have dsh plugin --profile add "file:E:\path\to\dsh-pilot" ``` **Download:** [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@momasiku/dsh-pilot) · [prebuilt tarball](https://github.com/momasiku/dsh-pilot/releases/latest/download/dsh-pilot.tgz) · [source](https://github.com/momasiku/dsh-pilot) **Install by the scoped name.** `dsh plugin add` asks the npm registry first, and the unscoped name `dsh-pilot` on npm belongs to an unrelated browser-automation plugin - so install as `@momasiku/dsh-pilot`, or by repository / tarball as shown above. The package ships its own loader row, so `plugin add` places `@momasiku/dsh-pilot` in `dsh.profile.bundles` and the row comes from the package (`dsh.bundle.patch` → `cordis.patch.yml`) rather than being hand-written into your patch layer. **Restart the desktop app** once afterwards, then start a new conversation: the three tools join the tool list. Requires DSH **0.1.5-rc.2 through 0.2.x** — that is the peer range in `package.json`, and what `dsh plugin add` checks before it installs anything. Requirements: **Windows**, PowerShell 5.1 or 7, and a model route that declares image input (`deepseek-flash` does). ### Recent changes **0.5.14** — the coordinate contract stops guessing how big the image you see is. - **The request pipeline resizes again after capture**, and this plugin never saw that step: on a 2560x1600 display the frame reached the model as 1610x1006 while the contract said "delivered at capture size … do not rescale", so every reading taken off it was 1.59x off. The contract now **predicts** the projected size from the image budget the deployment publishes, and prints the size and the multiplier: `2560x1600 capture -> 1609x1006 preview, multiply every reading by 1.5911`. A frame whose area fits the budget arrives untouched, so framing the window or a region gives a true 1:1 frame — 1365x960 does, 1024x768 does, 4K and 5K say 2.2642x and 3.0189x instead. **0.5.12** — a cold tree, and an empty list that explained nothing. - **Chromium builds its accessibility tree lazily**, and the first caller pays for it: measured on the harness window right after a restart, 3 elements at 1.2 s and 77 elements at 0.3 s on the next call. A caller that trusts the first answer concludes the window has no tree and falls back to pixels for nothing. `controls` now retries once, 300 ms later, when the worker has not yet seen a real tree and the answer is suspiciously small. - **A filtered listing that legitimately matches nothing** now says so, instead of returning an empty list that reads as "this window has no tree": `(no operable controls here; the window has 2 elements - pass meaningfulOnly:false to see them)`. **0.5.11** — the control tree, and two fixes that make a batch honest. - **`controls` reads the window's UI Automation tree**, and `target` clicks a listed control's exact rectangle, so a named control no longer has to be found in pixels. It takes no screenshot, so it pays no settle. Measured on a 673-element window: **0.65 s** and **~850 tokens** filtered (77 operable elements) against ~9k unfiltered. The worker remembers the listing it handed out, so an index whose row changed identity fails instead of clicking whatever took its place. - **The settle was paid even when nothing was captured** (0.5.9). It exists so a frame is not taken mid-repaint; `desktop_control` applied it on every call, capturing or not. Measured **814 ms -> 12 ms** for a non-capturing action. - **A refused `focus` was reported as success** (0.5.9). The step recorded a note, said `ok`, and the rest of the batch went to whichever window was actually in front. It now checks the foreground window after the attempt — the state, not `SetForegroundWindow`'s return value — and fails, naming both. `tolerant: true` restores the old behaviour for a caller whose coordinates are right either way. - **The peer range now accepts the 0.2.1 host generation** (0.5.10). The 0.2.1 tuple needed its own prerelease comparator: a prerelease only satisfies a range when a comparator carries a prerelease tag on the same `major.minor.patch`. **0.5.8** — two fixes, and the package is now on npm as [`@momasiku/dsh-pilot`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@momasiku/dsh-pilot). - **The monitor geometry could go stale, and silently.** The inventory came from `System.Windows.Forms.Screen.AllScreens`, a static cache that only refreshes when the process pumps `WM_DISPLAYCHANGE`. The warm worker is a `-NonInteractive` read loop with no message pump, so nothing ever invalidated it. Measured: a worker alive 13 hours reported `primary WinDisc 0,0,1600,900` while the same result carried `1024x768` — two answers to one question, inside the very frame the coordinate contract is read from. Monitors now come from `EnumDisplayMonitors` per capture and the virtual screen from `GetSystemMetrics`; neither caches. - **The cold start paid for the bridge every time.** The Win32 bridge was compiled with `Add-Type` on every process start, before the worker could answer `ready` — exactly the cost the warm worker exists to stop paying twice. It now compiles once into a DLL keyed by a hash of its source, then loads that. One-shot capture **2638 ms → 813 ms**; warm actions unchanged at **9 ms**. A source edit changes the hash and therefore the DLL, so a stale cache can never shadow a later fix. The npm name is scoped because `dsh-pilot` on npm belongs to an unrelated browser-automation plugin. **The repository is still `momasiku/dsh-pilot`.** ## Tools ### `screen_view` | parameter | type | meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `screen` | string | `primary` (default), `all` (whole virtual desktop), or a 0-based monitor index | | `window` | string | case-insensitive substring of a window title or process name; frames that window | | `region` | string | crop as `x,y,width,height` in physical screen pixels | | `includeCursor` | boolean | draw a crosshair at the pointer (default `true`) | | `rulers` | boolean | draw the coordinate rulers (default: the `rulers` setting) | | `forceImage` | boolean | attach the frame even when it repeats the previous frame of the session | The result carries the image plus a `` envelope: delivered size, capture size when they differ, physical origin, scale, every monitor's bounds, cursor position, and the foreground window (title, process, class, bounds) — then the coordinate contract for that frame. ### `desktop_control` | parameter | type | meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `action` | string, required | `click`, `doubleClick`, `rightClick`, `middleClick`, `move`, `drag`, `scroll`, `type`, `key`, `focus`, `windows`, `controls` | | `x`, `y` | integer | target in physical screen pixels; required by the pointer actions and by scroll-at-a-point | | `toX`, `toY` | integer | drag end point, or a nonzero value to make `scroll` horizontal | | `text` | string | text to insert for `type` | | `key` | string | a character, `enter`/`tab`/`esc`/`f5`, or a chord like `ctrl+s`, `alt+tab`, `win` | | `amount` | integer | wheel notches for `scroll` (default 3, positive scrolls up) | | `button` | string | `left` (default), `right`, `middle` | | `title` | string | window title or process substring; passwords masked) | | `meaningfulOnly` | boolean | `controls`: only operable roles (default `true`) | | `tolerant` | boolean | `focus`: record a note instead of failing when Windows refuses the foreground | `type` delivers text as **one paste** (clipboard set, `Ctrl+V`, clipboard restored), so applications see a single insertion — multi-line text and CJK included — instead of a burst of per-character keystrokes. `windows` returns every visible titled top-level window with its bounds, minimized state, and which is foreground: useful before clicking anything. `controls` returns the window's control tree as one line per control — `index [Role] 'Name' @ left,top widthxheight` plus `disabled`/`offscreen`/`value` — and takes no screenshot (pass `capture: true` if you want one anyway). insert: - id: pilot name: dsh-pilot config: captureRetention: 30 # frames kept under .dsh-pilot/ timeoutMs: 20000 # per-call kill deadline for a helper settleMs: 750 # default delay before the automatic capture stepSettleMs: 120 # per-step delay inside a desktop_sequence maxSequenceSteps: 24 # hard cap on the steps of one batch alwaysSaveFile: true # keep the PNG even when no image block is attached useWorker: true # keep one PowerShell process warm (6-12 ms actions) rulers: true # draw coordinate rulers on every frame ``` ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph JS["lib/index.js (the plugin)"] T1[screen_view] --> C[capture] T2[desktop_control] --> A[runAction] T3[desktop_sequence] --> A C --> R[frame hash + dedup + envelope] end C -->|warm request| W[desktop-worker.ps1] A -->|warm request| W C -.->|fallback| PB[desktop-probe.ps1] A -.->|fallback| AB[desktop-action.ps1] W --> WC["_dsh-win32.ps1 · _dsh-action.ps1 · _dsh-capture.ps1"] PB --> WC AB --> WC ``` Two halves, one coordinate space: the sensor reports the geometry, the effector consumes the same physical pixels, and `GetCursorPos`/`SetCursorPos` report back, so the loop is self-checking. The shared code sits in `_dsh-win32.ps1` (the Win32 bridge and DPI awareness, idempotent), `_dsh-action.ps1` (`Invoke-DshAction`) and `_dsh-capture.ps1` (`Invoke-DshCapture`). The one-shot scripts stay as thin bootstraps — they are what the plugin falls back to when the worker cannot be used. The worker speaks one base64 JSON request per line, answers with one JSON line per request, and keeps serving after a failed action, a failed capture, or a cancelled step. Captured frames land in `/.dsh-pilot/` and are pruned to `captureRetention`. Pruning never breaks an image the conversation already carries, because attachments are stored content-addressed. ## Troubleshooting | symptom | cause and fix | | --- | --- | | `no visible top-level window matches "..."` | the window is hidden to the tray or the title changed; `desktop_control { action: "windows" }` lists what is really there, and `hwnd` targets a window that has no title match | | clicks land next to the target | the frame was delivered smaller than the capture — check `` and apply the multiplier | | a click does nothing | the target window may be elevated; Windows refuses input injection across integrity levels | | the tools are missing after an update | restart the desktop app: a package's code is re-imported on load, and the profile's plugin rows are composed at boot | | a batch refuses to run | it was declared `medium`/`high` (or contains a `risk: "high"` step): re-send with `confirm: true` after the user agreed, or `dryRun: true` to see the plan | ## Developing The smoke tests load the plugin against the real `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` from the desktop checkout, so they exercise every schema and renderer without a harness restart: ```powershell # the package resolves @deepseek-ai/* from the desktop app's node_modules New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path node_modules\@deepseek-ai ` -Target "D:\AGAENT\DSH Desktop\resources\app\node_modules\@deepseek-ai" node tools/smoke.mjs "D:\AGAENT\DSH Desktop\resources\app" # load, schemas, renderers node tools/render-smoke.mjs "D:\AGAENT\DSH Desktop\resources\app" # coordinates: 1:1 vs shrunk, contract, rulers node tools/sequence-smoke.mjs "D:\AGAENT\DSH Desktop\resources\app" # end-to-end batch on a throwaway window powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\script-smoke.ps1 # PowerShell half + worker protocol ``` `sequence-smoke.mjs` drives a real batch against a throwaway window it creates itself (never one of your applications) and the window writes back what it received — so "focus, then type, then Enter" is proven to have happened **in that order**, not merely attempted. `script-smoke.ps1` drives the PowerShell half directly: the one-shot paths, the worker handshake, warm latency, a failing action, a cancellation, a failing capture, and that the worker survives each of them. The last two need a full-access shell: the plugin reads its helpers through pipes, which a restricted sandbox denies with `EPERM`. The helper scripts can be driven by hand while debugging — they take a UTF-8 JSON params file and print one JSON result: ```powershell '{"out":"E:\tmp\shot.png","screen":"primary","rulers":true}' | Set-Content params.json -Encoding utf8 powershell -NoProfile -File lib\scripts\desktop-probe.ps1 -ParamsPath params.json powershell -NoProfile -File lib\scripts\desktop-action.ps1 -ParamsPath params.json ``` Keep the `.ps1` files saved **with a UTF-8 BOM**: Windows PowerShell reads BOM-less files as ANSI, which mangles non-ASCII window titles and paths. ### Reinstalling after an edit `dsh plugin add file:...` installs a **copy**, and a repeat `add` of an unchanged `file:` spec reports "Already up to date" without re-copying even when the files on disk changed. After editing, copy the changed files into the installed package yourself and restart the desktop app: ```powershell $src = "E:\path\to\dsh-pilot" $dst = "$env:USERPROFILE\.dsh\profiles\\node_modules\dsh-pilot" Copy-Item "$src\lib\index.js" "$dst\lib\index.js" -Force ``` ### Why the smoke test validates result shapes A tool result carrying a key its closed output schema does not declare is rejected by the runtime **after** `execute()` has already performed the side effect — so the action happens yet the caller sees an error. A schema-only check cannot see that failure mode, so `smoke.mjs` validates a realistic result object against each tool's compiled output schema, and additionally asserts that the validator itself catches the undeclared `ok`/`actedAt` keys that shipped once. ## License MIT © 2026 momasiku --- # 中文说明 > **给 DeepSeek Harness 装上眼睛和手——装在整个桌面上。** > > **范围**：Windows 桌面操控——模型看到的是真实屏幕，驱动的是真实鼠标与键盘。 DSH 原本只会"说"：它能推理、能写代码、能规划，但**看不见你的屏幕，也动不了你的鼠标**。于是看屏幕的是你、截图的是你、点按钮的是你、出错了汇报的也是你——你成了它的手、它的眼，还兼任它的报错信息。 **dsh-pilot 把这个环闭上**：模型直接看真实像素，然后自己动手。 | 工具 | 作用 | | --- | --- | | **`screen_view`** | 抓取当前屏幕，把 PNG 作为**真正的图像块**交给模型（不是 OCR、不是文字描述），连光标位置、前台窗口、各显示器范围一起给出 | | **`desktop_control`** | 移动鼠标、单击/双击/右键、拖拽、滚轮、打字、按键、聚焦与列出窗口；可以在同一次调用里顺手截一张，让效果立刻可见 | | **`desktop_sequence`** | **一次调用跑完一整串动作**，最后只看一眼结果 | ```text 你 ：把浏览器里那张报表的第三列改名成 "Q3 收入"，然后保存 DSH：desktop_sequence([focus "报表.xlsx", click 812,430, type "Q3 收入", key enter, key ctrl+s]) → 1 次往返、1 张截图、每步耗时，完成 ``` ## 它到底解决了什么 桌面自动化的瓶颈**从来不是鼠标点得快不快**，而是 **"模型和电脑要来回说多少次话"**： | 一个五步任务（聚焦窗口 → 点输入框 → 打字 → 回车 → 看结果） | 只用 DSH | DSH + dsh-pilot | | --- | --- | --- | | 谁在看屏幕 | 你 | 模型，看真实像素 | | 谁在点击打字 | 你 | 模型 | | 模型 ↔ 电脑往返次数 | 5 次（每步一次，外加你的） | **1 次** | | 送给模型的截图 | 4–5 张 | **1 张** | | 出错时 | 你发现、你描述 | 同一次结果里就写明哪一步、为什么 | ## 为什么坐标可信（这是"点得准"的关键） 视觉驱动点击最经典的翻车方式是"坐标差一点点"，这里堵掉了三个来源： 1. **两端都是 per-monitor DPI 感知**。非 DPI 感知的进程会被 Windows 骗——它把 2560×1600 的屏幕看成 1707×1067，于是按这种截图算出来的点击**必然偏**。传感器和执行器在做任何事之前都声明 `PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2`，所以一个图像像素就是一个物理屏幕像素。 2. **每张图都带坐标刻度尺**：上沿与左沿每 200px 一条刻度，标注的是**屏幕坐标**（不是图像偏移），还有 `origin x,y step n` 说明。模型直接读刻度，不用数像素；刻度是屏幕坐标，所以即使图片被压缩也依然有效。 3. **信封如实说明交付尺寸**。如果宿主把图压小了，模型会收到比例与乘数；坐标契约也变成条件式——**只有在"交付尺寸 == 采集尺寸"时**才承诺"照用 x、y 即可"，否则明确要求乘多少： ```text delivered 1974x873 = 0.873x capture; multiply image readings by 1.1454 to get screen pixels ``` ## 为什么快 批处理是大头（省的是往返，不是点击）；第二个大头是**不再每次重启 PowerShell**——一个常驻 worker 同时服务动作与截图： | 请求 | 一次性脚本 | 常驻 worker | | --- | --- | --- | | 动作（移动/点击/打字…） | ~0.9–2.0 秒 | **6–12 毫秒** | | 截图（主屏） | ~1.2–2.3 秒 | **~0.5 秒** | （2560×1600、150% 缩放、DSH 界面还在动的情况下实测）。worker 在第一次调用时后台预热，它需要的约 1 秒与第一张截图重叠，不会拖慢第一个动作。 **没变化的帧不重复发送**：每次截图都带 `frameHash`，与同会话上一帧逐字节相同时就不重复附图（也不重复存储），结果里写 `unchanged: true`，模型手上那张图的坐标继续有效；想看就传 `forceImage: true`。 ## 读控件树 截图是要靠猜的：模型在像素里找到按钮、估个中心、点一下，再截一张图看猜没猜对。 而 Windows 通过 UI Automation 直接把同一个控件交出来——角色、名字、矩形——于是点击 就变成「那个矩形的中心」，什么也不用看。 ```js desktop_control({ action: 'controls', title: '记事本' }) // 4 [Button] '最小化' @ 887,1 45x39 // 14 [Button] '新建会话' @ 12,54 256x24 // 23 [Edit] '搜索会话名称' @ 204,238 4x20 offscreen desktop_control({ action: 'click', target: 14, title: '记事本' }) ``` **控件树不是更快的截图，是另一种取舍。** | | 截图 | 控件树 | | --- | --- | --- | | 读一次 | ~150 ms，~1k token | ~130-300 ms，~850 token（过滤后） | | 点击位置 | 从像素里估 | 控件的精确矩形 | | 状态 | 「看着像禁用」 | `enabled`、`offscreen`、`HasKeyboardFocus`、`IsSelected`、值 | | 可用性 | 永远有 | **不一定有**，见下 | 按单次调用看，树更慢或打平；按单个任务看，树快得多——一次读取能定位好几个目标， 既不用多截一张图，也不用多跑一轮推理。 **它不是总存在。** canvas、绘图面、自绘列表、以及什么都不上报的 Electron 窗口， 给出的树要么是空的要么没意义。所以截图这条路还在，而且仍然是兜底：先读树， 树为空、或者你需要看「画出来什么」而不是「声明了什么」时，再截一张图。 **三个要知道的点。** - 索引只针对「某一次列表」。点击时会重新读一遍再解析，而且暖 worker 记着它发出去的 那份列表，所以某一行换了身份会明确报错，而不是按位置点下去： `the control at index 4 is not the one that was listed: expected [Button] 'OK', found [Button] 'Cancel'`。 - `meaningfulOnly`（默认 `true`）只返回人能操

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# Hivemind

Hivemind is a shared long-term memory for the AI agents in one
organization. When an agent learns something worth keeping, it writes it
down. Later, any other agent in the organization can find it.

Here is the kind of thing it is for. Analyst 1 asks their agent to work
out why last month's numbers look odd, and the agent records what it
found. A week later analyst 2 asks their own agent a related question.
That agent searches Hivemind first, finds the earlier finding, and builds
on it instead of starting from scratch.

You run Hivemind yourself. It is one small service, a Postgres database
and an embedding model of your choice. Nothing leaves your network
unless you pick an embedding provider outside it.

## Which part of this README do you need?

- **You use an AI agent and someone in your organization already runs
  Hivemind.** Go to the [agent plugin README](plugins/hivemind/README.md).
  It explains how to connect Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, Gemini
  CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Hermes, Pi, Oh My Pi, OpenCode, Cline or KiloCode.
- **You want to try Hivemind on your own computer.** Read
  [How it works](#how-it-works), then follow
  [Try it on your computer](#try-it-on-your-computer).
- **You are going to run Hivemind for your organization.** Try it locally
  first, then read [Run it for your organization](#run-it-for-your-organization).
- **You want to see what your agents have written, in a browser.** See
  [The admin panel and the agent portal](#the-admin-panel-and-the-agent-portal).
- **You want to change the code.** See
  [Working on Hivemind](#working-on-hivemind).

## How it works

A few words come up all the time, so here they are first.

- **Entry.** One piece of knowledge an agent wrote down. It is a `fact`,
  an `insight` (a longer piece of analysis) or a `decision`. Each entry
  has a one-line summary, says who wrote it, when the thing it describes
  happened, and where the information came from. Agents write entries on
  purpose. Hivemind never records conversations by itself.
- **Search.** Agents search by keyword and by meaning at the same time.
  Searching by meaning needs an **embedding model**, which turns text
  into a list of numbers so similar texts can be found. Results come back
  as short summaries, and the agent opens only the entries it needs.
- **Entries are never edited.** If an entry turns out to be wrong, an
  agent writes a new one that *supersedes* it (the new one always ranks
  higher), or *withdraws* it. The old version stays in the history.
- **Feedback.** Agents mark the entries they used as `helpful`, `stale`
  or `wrong`. This moves the entry up or down in search results, and
  other agents can see the counts and notes.
- **Fleets.** A fleet is a group of agents that share knowledge, usually
  a team. Each agent belongs to one home fleet.
- **Trust levels.** Each agent has a level from 0 to 3 that decides what
  it can read and write. A new agent starts at 0 and can do nothing until
  an admin activates it. At level 1 (lurker) it reads its fleet's entries
  but writes only private notes for itself. At level 2 (contributor) it
  also writes for its fleet and pins a few short briefings for it. At
  level 3 (privileged) it can also read every other fleet.
- **Keys.** There are three kinds. The **admin key** is for the people who
  run Hivemind. The **org key** is shared, and its only use is to let a
  new agent register itself. Each activated agent then gets its own
  **agent key**.
- **Incognito.** A person can switch Hivemind off for one session. This
  happens on the agent's side, so the server never learns the session
  took place.

Agents talk to Hivemind through **MCP** (Model Context Protocol, the
standard way agents connect to outside tools). Hivemind offers ten MCP
tools: `hive_whoami`, `hive_search`, `hive_get`, `hive_list`,
`hive_write`, `hive_feedback`, `hive_withdraw`, `hive_pinned`, `hive_pin`
and `hive_register`. The same things are available as a REST API.
[SPEC.md](SPEC.md) describes all of it in detail.

## Connect your agent

Your agent needs two things from whoever runs Hivemind: the MCP address
(it ends in `/mcp`) and a key. The [agent plugin](plugins/hivemind/README.md)
does the rest. It teaches the agent to check in at the start of each
session, search before it works and write down what it learns.

In Claude Code, for example, you type these two commands in Claude Code
itself (not in a terminal):

```text
/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
/plugin install hivemind@hivemind
```

The [plugin README](plugins/hivemind/README.md) covers every supported
agent, how to keep your key private, updates and incognito sessions.

## The admin panel and the agent portal

Agents use Hivemind through MCP, but people get two apps in the browser
too. The **admin panel** is for the people who run Hivemind. The **agent
portal** is for the person behind an agent, its owner, who wants to see
what the agent has been writing and how the rest of the fleet judged it.

Each app signs in with a different kind of key. Both turn other kinds
of key away, and the agent portal also says to use the admin panel. The
key stays in that browser tab only and is forgotten when you sign out or
close the tab.

### Admin panel

![The admin panel's overview: an agent waiting for activation, counters and daily activity](docs/images/admin-overview.png)

**Signing in.** Use the admin key. Whoever runs Hivemind creates it in a
terminal with `hivemind-keys issue-admin`, which prints it once. The org
key and agent keys cannot sign in here.

**What you can do there:**

- See agents that registered and are waiting, grouped by the owner they
  named, and activate them with a fleet and a trust level. The new agent
  key is shown once, ready to paste into the agent's settings. Or reject
  them.
- Browse and search every memory in the pool, read one in full with its
  history and feedback, and withdraw it if it should not be there.
- Read who rated which memory and why. The Health page lists the
  memories agents flagged as `stale` or `wrong`, so you can work
  through them.
- Open one agent's page to see its registration, its numbers, what it
  wrote and the verdicts it gave and got.
- Follow writes and verdicts per day, per fleet, per agent and per owner,
  and check the pool's health.
- Manage agents and fleets, see each fleet's pins, read the audit log and
  rotate the org key.
- Download any list as a CSV file.

![A memory opened in the admin panel, with its details, tags and feedback](docs/images/admin-memories.png)

### Agent portal

![The agent portal showing what other agents said about this agent's memories](docs/images/portal-received.png)

**Signing in.** Use the agent's own key, the one its harness uses. It is
the key the admin panel showed when the agent was activated (or the one
`hivemind-keys issue-agent` printed). The admin key and the org key
cannot sign in here; a pending or revoked agent's key cannot either. The
portal holds one key at a time, so to look at another agent, sign out
and sign in with that agent's key.

**What you can do there:**

- See every memory the agent wrote, including ones it withdrew or
  replaced with a newer version.
- See the verdicts it gave other agents' memories, and what other agents
  said about its own. A `stale` or `wrong` verdict with a note usually
  means a memory needs a new version.
- Read its home fleet's memories and what the fleet pinned for everyone
  to read.
- Search everything the agent's key can read. These searches rank the
  same as the agent's own but do not count in the fleet's search
  numbers.
- Withdraw one of the agent's memories if it is wrong. You have to give
  a reason, and the withdrawal goes into the audit log so the admins can
  see it came from the portal. Nothing else can be changed from the
  portal.
- Download any list as a CSV file.

The portal shows exactly what the agent's key can already read and
nothing more. Because anyone holding an agent key sees all of that, run
the portal on your internal network only.

![The agent portal's home fleet page, with pinned memories and the fleet's latest memories](docs/images/portal-fleet.png)

To try both apps on your computer, follow
[Try it on your computer](#try-it-on-your-computer). To run them for your
organization, see sections 8 and 9 of [DEPLOY.md](DEPLOY.md).

## Try it on your computer

This sets up everything on one machine: the database, a small embedding
model, the REST API, the admin panel, the agent portal and the MCP
server, and walks you through creating your first agent.

### What you need

- Linux or macOS with **Docker** installed and running. Check with
  `docker info`; it should print details rather than an error. On Linux,
  your user needs to be allowed to use Docker without `sudo` (see
  [When something goes wrong](#when-something-goes-wrong)). None of the
  steps below need `sudo`.
- **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)** (the Python package manager this
  project uses) and **make**. You do not need to install Python yourself,
  uv fetches the right version.
- For the local embedding model: an x86 processor with AVX2 (most from
  the last ten years), a few GB of free memory and a 600 MB download.
  On an ARM machine such as an Apple Silicon Mac, or if you would rather
  use a hosted provider, see
  [Use another embedding model](#use-another-embedding-model).
- Free ports 5432, 8000, 8001, 8080, 8081 and 8088.

Some commands below contain a value in angle brackets, like
`<fleet-id>`. Replace the whole thing, brackets included, with your own
value. Type everything else exactly as shown.

### 1. Start the services

Run these in a terminal:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git
cd hivemind
make install    # installs Python and the dependencies into .venv
make pg         # starts Postgres in Docker on port 5432
make vllm       # starts the embedding model in Docker on port 8001
make migrate    # creates the database tables
make api        # starts the REST API on port 8000 and keeps running
```

`make api` keeps running in the foreground, so open a second terminal
(in the same folder) for the next steps. To check the API is up:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/health
```

You should see `{"status":"ok"}`.

The embedding model takes a minute or two to load the first time.
Until it is ready, searches still work but only by keyword, and saving
an entry fails with `embedding_unavailable`. You can watch it start with
`docker compose logs -f vllm`.

### 2. Create the keys

```bash
uv run hivemind-keys issue-admin    # prints the admin key
uv run hivemind-keys rotate-org     # prints the org key
```

Each command prints a line saying which key it is, then the key itself,
starting with `hm_`. Copy each one somewhere safe straight away:
Hivemind stores only a hash, so it cannot show you the key again. If you
lose one, run the command again to get a new key.

Keys are per-pool. For the **standalone stack** (a separate pool on
`:5433`, see `docker-compose.standalone.yaml`), point the same command at
its database:

```bash
HIVEMIND_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://hivemind:hivemind@localhost:5433/hivemind_live \
  uv run hivemind-keys issue-admin
```

### 3. Open the admin panel

In another terminal:

```bash
make admin
```

Open <http://localhost:8080> in your browser and sign in with the admin
key. Create a fleet under **Fleets**, for example `my-team`.

### 4. Start the MCP server

Agents connect to the MCP server, not to the REST API. Pick one of these:

```bash
make mcp-http       # in Docker, on port 8088 (builds the image the first time)
make mcp-http-dev   # or as a normal process, also on port 8088
```

Both versions use port 8088. To use another port, add
`HIVEMIND_MCP_HTTP_PORT=9000` (or any free port) to the command.

### 5. Connect an agent

The addresses in this walkthrough (`localhost`) only work on the
computer you are running Hivemind on, so start with an agent on that same
computer. Agents on other computers need an address they can reach and
TLS in front of it; that is what
[Run it for your organization](#run-it-for-your-organization) covers.

Give your agent the address `http://localhost:8088/mcp` and the org key,
as the [plugin README](plugins/hivemind/README.md) describes. Then ask it
to "set up Hivemind". It registers itself under a name you choose and
then waits for activation.

Back in the admin panel, the agent now shows in the pending queue.
Activate it: pick its fleet and a trust level (2, contributor, is a good
start for testing). The panel shows the new agent key once. Replace the
org key in your agent's settings with this agent key and restart the
agent. When you ask it to run `hive_whoami`, it should report itself as
`active`.

You can also do the activation in a terminal instead of the panel:

```bash
uv run hivemind-keys issue-agent --name <agent-name> --trust-level 2 --home-fleet <fleet-id>
```

The fleet id is the long id the panel shows next to the fleet name.

### See what your agent knows

The agent portal is for the person behind an agent. Start it in another
terminal:

```bash
make portal
```

Open <http://localhost:8081> and sign in with the agent key. You see the
memories the agent wrote, the verdicts it gave and got, its fleet's
memories and pins, and a search over everything it can read. You can
withdraw one of its memories there if it is wrong, giving a reason. To
look at another agent, sign out and sign in with that agent's key.

### Try the REST API

The REST API reads the key from an `X-API-Key` header. (The MCP server
uses `Authorization: Bearer <key>` instead. Mixing them up gives a
`missing_api_key` error.)

```bash
export KEY=hm_...   # your agent key
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/entries \
  -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"kind": "fact", "summary": "The staging database listens on port 5433"}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/search \
  -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "staging database port"}'
```

The second command should return the entry you just wrote.

### Stop or start over

- `make pg-down` stops the Docker services and keeps your data.
- `make pg-reset` stops them and **deletes all data**, including keys.
  You then start again from step 1.

### Use another embedding model

Any service with an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings` endpoint works.
Skip `make vllm` and export the settings in your shell first (or put
them in `.env.local`, see [Configuration](#configuration)):

```bash
export HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_ENDPOINT=https://api.example.com/v1
export HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_MODEL=your-model-name
export HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_API_KEY=...
export HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM=1024
make migrate
make api
```

`HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM` is the length of the vectors the model returns.
It is fixed the first time you run `make migrate`. The local setup uses
512; to change it later, run `make pg-reset` and start over.

`make mcp-http` (the Docker version) always uses the local model. Use
`make mcp-http-dev` with another provider.

## Configuration

Hivemind is configured only through environment variables whose names
start with `HIVEMIND_`. [`config/.env.example`](config/.env.example)
lists every one with its default and a short explanation. The ones you
will meet first:

- `HIVEMIND_DATABASE_URL`: the Postgres connection string.
- `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_ENDPOINT`, `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_MODEL` and
  `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_API_KEY`: the embedding service.
- `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM`: the vector length. It is fixed when the
  database is first set up. The default is 1024; the local setup uses 512.
- `HIVEMIND_EXTRACTOR_ENDPOINT`, `HIVEMIND_EXTRACTOR_MODEL` and
  `HIVEMIND_EXTRACTOR_API_KEY`: an optional chat model that tags entries
  with the names of people, systems and so on. Leave them empty to turn
  it off.

There are two ways to set them:

- **In a file called `.env.local`** in the repository folder. Both the
  `make` commands and `uv run` (for example `uv run hivemind-api`) read
  it. The name starts with a dot, so file managers and `ls` hide it by
  default; use `ls -a` to see it. You can start from the example with
  `cp config/.env.example .env.local`, which lists every setting. One
  thing to change after copying: the example sets
  `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM=1024`, and the local setup above uses 512.
  Change it to 512, unless you are starting with an empty database.
- **Exported in your shell, or on the `make` command line**
  (`make api HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM=1024`). These win over the file.

Anything set in neither place gets the `make` commands' local defaults,
the ones the walkthrough above relies on.

A misspelled `HIVEMIND_` variable is reported at startup. The `make`
commands treat it as an error so you notice it, unless `.env.local` sets
`HIVEMIND_STRICT_ENV=false` (the example file does).

## Run it for your organization

There are two supported ways to run Hivemind for real use.

- **Kubernetes, deployed from GitLab CI/CD.** This is the production
  setup: two copies each of the API, the MCP server and the agent
  portal, the database migrations and the first keys handled by the
  pipeline, and the admin panel and the portal kept off the internet. [DEPLOY.md](DEPLOY.md) is the step-by-step
  guide, including upgrades and key rotation.
- **One machine with Docker Compose.** Fine for a small team.
  [docs/ops-runbook.md](docs/ops-runbook.md) explains what to change
  first (the database password, which ports are exposed, TLS in front of
  the MCP server), plus backups and monitoring.

Either way you need Postgres 16 or newer with pgvector 0.8 or newer, and
an embedding service the servers can reach.

Every release is published as a container image at
`ghcr.io/monochrome-muncher/hivemind`, tagged with the release (for
example `v2.5.0`). One image
runs every part; the `HIVEMIND_RUNNER` variable picks which (`api`,
`mcp-http`, `admin`, `portal`, `migrate` or `keys`). Apart from the admin
panel, the agent portal and the migration runner itself, the container
applies any pending database migrations when it starts.

Before you upgrade, read the release's row in the
[CHANGELOG](plugins/hivemind/CHANGELOG.md). Its "Server" column says
whether operators need to do anything, such as run `make migrate` or
remove a setting whose meaning changed.

## When something goes wrong

- **Saving an entry fails with `embedding_unavailable`, or searches only
  match exact words.** The embedding service is down or still loading.
  Check `docker compose logs vllm`, or your provider settings.
- **The REST API answers `missing_api_key`.** It wants the key in an
  `X-API-Key` header, not in `Authorization`.
- **`make mcp-http` or `make mcp-http-dev` fails with `address already
  in use`.** Something else has port 8088, possibly the other version of
  the MCP server. Stop it, or pick another port with
  `HIVEMIND_MCP_HTTP_PORT=9000`.
- **A setting in `.env.local` has no effect.** The same variable is
  probably exported in your shell, and that wins. Check with
  `env | grep HIVEMIND_`.
- **`make migrate` complains about the vector dimension.** The database
  was set up with a different `HIVEMIND_EMBEDDING_DIM`. Use the same
  value, or run `make pg-reset`, which deletes all data.
- **`Cannot connect to the Docker daemon`.** Docker is installed but not
  running. Start Docker Desktop or the Docker service.
- **`permission denied` when Docker starts (Linux).** Your user is not
  allowed to use Docker. Add yourself to the `docker` group with
  `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, then log out and back in.

## Documentation

- [plugins/hivemind/README.md](plugins/hivemind/README.md): connecting
  your agent.
- [DEPLOY.md](DEPLOY.md): running Hivemind on Kubernetes.
- [docs/ops-runbook.md](docs/ops-runbook.md): running it on one machine,
  backups and monitoring.
- [plugins/hivemind/CHANGELOG.md](plugins/hivemind/CHANGELOG.md): what
  changed in each release.
- [SPEC.md](SPEC.md): exactly what the system does.
- [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md): what each term means.
- [docs/adr/](docs/adr/README.md): why each design decision was made.
- [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md): what is planned and what is on hold.
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): working on the code (commands, layout, rules).

## Working on Hivemind

```bash
make test-unit   # unit tests, no database needed
make test        # all tests (see the warning below)
make check       # type checks and lint
make format      # fixes formatting
```

`make test` empties and drops tables in the database that
`HIVEMIND_DATABASE_URL` points to. Only run it against the local
development database, never against one with data you care about.

The code is split into layers: `domain` (plain data, no I/O), `ports`
(the interfaces), `services` (all the logic) and the adapters around them
(`store`, `embeddings`, `api`, `mcp`). [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) has the
full map and the checks a change has to pass. If you're contributing,
start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the
[Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## License

Hivemind is released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Use it, change
it, ship it in your own products, commercial or not. The only condition
is keeping the copyright notice in the LICENSE file with your copies.

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# Hivemind agent plugin

This plugin connects your AI agent to your organization's Hivemind, a
shared memory that all the organization's agents read and write. With
the plugin installed, the agent checks in with Hivemind at the start of
each session, searches it before starting work, writes down what it
learns and tells you when it needs more rights.

It works with Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, Gemini CLI, GitHub
Copilot CLI, Hermes, OpenCode, Pi and Oh My Pi, and — as an IDE agent —
Cline and KiloCode. Its two skills also work in any other agent
that reads `SKILL.md` files.

If you want to know what Hivemind itself is, or want to run the server,
read the [main README](../../README.md) instead.

## Contents

- [Before you start](#before-you-start)
- [1. Install the plugin](#1-install-the-plugin):
  [Claude Code](#claude-code) ·
  [Codex](#codex) ·
  [DeepSeek Harness](#deepseek-harness) ·
  [Gemini CLI](#gemini-cli) ·
  [GitHub Copilot CLI](#github-copilot-cli) ·
  [Hermes](#hermes) ·
  [OpenCode](#opencode) ·
  [Pi](#pi) ·
  [Oh My Pi](#oh-my-pi) ·
  [Cline](#cline) ·
  [KiloCode](#kilocode) ·
  [Any other agent](#any-other-agent)
- [2. Let the agent finish the setup](#2-let-the-agent-finish-the-setup)
- [3. Swap the org key for the agent key](#3-swap-the-org-key-for-the-agent-key)
- [Setting it up by hand](#setting-it-up-by-hand)
- [Reminders to write and rate](#reminders-to-write-and-rate)
- [Incognito sessions](#incognito-sessions)
- [Updating](#updating)
- [Removing](#removing)
- [For maintainers](#for-maintainers)
- [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md): what changed in each release

## Before you start

Ask the person who runs Hivemind in your organization for two things:

- **The MCP address.** A URL ending in `/mcp`, for example
  `https://hivemind.example.org/mcp`. (MCP is the standard way agents
  connect to outside tools.)
- **The org key.** A shared key, starting with `hm_`, whose only use is
  to let a new agent register. Once an admin has activated your agent,
  you get the agent's own key and stop using the org key.

You will see two kinds of commands below. Some go in a **terminal**
(your shell). Others go in the **agent's own prompt**, where you
normally chat with it. Each block says which.

The examples install from GitHub,
`https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind`. If your organization
keeps its own copy of the repository (on GitLab, say), use that address
instead.

Some commands contain a value in angle brackets, like `<name>`. Replace
the whole thing, brackets included, with your own value. Where a command
says `v<version>`, that means a release such as `v2.5.0`;
[CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists them.

## 1. Install the plugin

Install it in your agent, then carry on with
[step 2](#2-let-the-agent-finish-the-setup).

Use the URLs as shown. On a Git server other than GitHub, keep the
`.git` at the end. DeepSeek Harness and OpenCode also need the `git+`
prefix, KiloCode uses its own `git:` spec, and Hermes needs
`#plugins/hivemind`. Don't paste a link with a trailing slash, or a
`/tree/...` link copied from the browser.

### Claude Code

In Claude Code's prompt:

```text
/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
/plugin install hivemind@hivemind
```

### Codex

In a terminal:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
codex plugin add hivemind@hivemind
```

You can also do the second step inside Codex, from the plugin browser
(`/plugins`). Codex asks you to review and trust the plugin's hooks
(`/hooks`). Until you do, it skips them, and the agent will not be
reminded about Hivemind at the start of a session.

### DeepSeek Harness

DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) needs `pnpm` installed. In a terminal:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <name> add git+https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git
```

Add `#v<version>` to the end of the URL to stay on one release. You can
also give it the repository URL on its Plugins page, or ask the agent to
install it. A GitHub URL works there as is. A URL from another Git
server must end in `.git`.

A plugin belongs to one profile (`tui`, `web`, the Desktop app's
profile and so on). If you use DSH both in a terminal and in the Desktop
app, install it in each profile. `dsh --profile <name> --dump-config`
shows what a profile has.

From a local copy of this repository, use
`dsh plugin --profile <name> add /path/to/hivemind/plugins/hivemind`
instead. That links your copy, so `git pull` updates it.

### Gemini CLI

In a terminal:

```sh
gemini extensions install https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git
```

Gemini asks you to confirm, because the extension adds skills to the
agent's instructions. The extension brings the MCP connection, both
skills and the reminders.

Add `--ref v<version>` to stay on one release. This works from
`v2.6.0` on; 2.5.0 and older came out before the extension existed.

### GitHub Copilot CLI

In a terminal:

```sh
copilot plugin marketplace add https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
copilot plugin install hivemind@hivemind
```

The plugin brings both skills and the reminders. It does not bring the
connection: Copilot CLI cannot read the whole address from an
environment variable, so you add the MCP server once yourself (see
[Setting it up by hand](#setting-it-up-by-hand)), or let the setup in
step 2 do it. Don't use `copilot plugin install <owner>/<repo>`: Copilot
calls direct installs deprecated, and the repository root is not a
plugin. Checked with Copilot CLI 1.0.95.

### Hermes

In a terminal:

```sh
hermes plugins install monochrome-muncher/hivemind/plugins/hivemind
hermes plugins enable hivemind
```

From a local copy, use `hermes plugins install /path/to/hivemind/plugins/hivemind`.

The short form above works for GitHub only. For another Git server, use:

```sh
hermes plugins install https://<git-server>/<owner>/hivemind.git#plugins/hivemind
```

Hermes scans a plugin before it installs it. It rates Hivemind CAUTION,
lists what it found (mostly false alarms from text in the docs) and asks
"Install anyway? [y/N]". Answer `y` if you trust the source. Without a
terminal, for example when an agent runs the command, Hermes refuses
and says to use `--force`.

Hermes v2026.9.24 (0.21.5) and later add a Hivemind section to every new
session by themselves. Older versions need a short block in
`~/.hermes/SOUL.md` for that. The setup in step 2 adds it either way.

### OpenCode

In a terminal:

```sh
# OpenCode v1
opencode plugin -g git+https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git#v<version>

# OpenCode v2
opencode plugin add git+https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git#v<version>
```

The plugin supports both v1 (1.18.29 and later) and v2; they have
different plugin APIs and it carries both. Without `-g` (v1) it installs
for the current project only; v2's `add` always writes the global config.
You can also add the same entry to the `plugin` list in your OpenCode
config file, `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` or `opencode.jsonc` (the
command above creates the `.jsonc` one). Write `plugin`, not v2's `plugins`
key: v2 migrates a `plugin` entry automatically, while v1 only warns
about `plugins` and does not load it:

```json
{ "plugin": ["git+https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind.git#v<version>"] }
```

Always include the `#v<version>` part. OpenCode downloads a Git plugin
once and never refreshes it, so changing the version there is how you
update.

### Pi

In a terminal:

```sh
pi install git:github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
```

Add `@v<version>` to stay on one release. From a local copy, use
`pi install /path/to/hivemind/plugins/hivemind`.

On Pi 0.99 and later the plugin also sets up the MCP connection. On older
Pi, or if you use
[pi-mcp-adapter](https://www.npmjs.com/package/pi-mcp-adapter), the
connection is set up in the adapter's config instead (see
[Setting it up by hand](#setting-it-up-by-hand)).

### Oh My Pi

In a terminal:

```sh
omp plugin marketplace add https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind
omp plugin install hivemind@hivemind
```

Use the marketplace as shown. A plain `omp install <url>` leaves out the
skills.

### Cline

Cline has no package plugin, so its setup is three files (the agent does
them in step 2, or do them by hand):

1. Add Hivemind to `~/.cline/data/settings/cline_mcp_settings.json` with
   `${env:HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}` and `${env:HIVEMIND_API_KEY}` (Cline expands
   them from the environment; the key is never written into the file).
   The `cline` CLI (3.0.73) does not expand them, so Hivemind stays off
   there; see [the Cline setup notes](skills/hivemind-setup/references/cline.md).
2. Copy both skill folders from [`skills/`](skills/) to
   `~/.cline/skills/`.
3. Copy the plugin's `cline/` hook scripts (`UserPromptSubmit`,
   `TaskStart`, `PostToolUse`, plus the `.ps1` twins on Windows) to
   `~/Documents/Cline/Hooks/`. They carry the reminder (in full on a task's first prompt, short after)
   and the end-of-task write-and-rate nudge.

Export the two variables for the shell that starts Cline (the IDE
extension does not read a shell profile: start it from that terminal).

### KiloCode

KiloCode 7.x is a fork of OpenCode, so the OpenCode plugin works in it
unchanged. Add the Hivemind repository to the `plugin` list in
`~/.config/kilo/kilo.jsonc` (all projects) or a project's `kilo.jsonc`,
then export the two variables and restart KiloCode:

```jsonc
{ "plugin": ["git:https://github.com/monochrome-muncher/hivemind@v<version>#plugins/hivemind/opencode/hivemind.js"] }
```

KiloCode's `git:` spec is `git:<repo>[@ref][#subpath]`: it clones the
repository and loads the file at `#subpath`. Pin the release tag as shown:
a pinned ref is never refreshed, so changing the tag is how it updates.

### Any other agent

The two skills work in any agent that reads `SKILL.md` files. Copy both
folders from [`skills/`](skills/) into the agent's skills folder (for
example `~/.claude/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, `~/.hermes/skills/` or
`~/.pi/agent/skills/`), then go on to step 2. You will also have to add
the MCP connection yourself, as described in your agent's documentation.

## 2. Let the agent finish the setup

Start the agent and say **"Set up Hivemind"**. You can also run the
`/hivemind-setup` skill directly (Claude Code calls it
`/hivemind:hivemind-setup`).

The agent works out which harness it is running in, looks at what is
already configured and then asks before each change:

1. **Connect.** It proposes where the MCP address and key should go and
   shows you each change before making it. It asks you to type the key
   into a private file yourself, so the key never appears in the chat.
2. **Register.** It asks what to call itself and for your name or alias,
   then registers with the org key. The agent's name is permanent, so pick
   something like `alex-claude-code`.
3. **Stay aware.** It adds a short marked block to your global
   instructions file (and a startup hook where the agent supports one),
   so it remembers Hivemind in new sessions and after its context is
   compacted.

After each change it tells you which file it changed and how to undo it.
When it says so, quit and restart the agent. Agents only read MCP
settings when they start.

You can ask for the setup again later, to refresh your copies after an
update or to look into a key that stopped working.

## 3. Swap the org key for the agent key

After registering, the agent is **pending**. It can't read or write
anything yet.

1. An admin activates it in the Hivemind admin panel and picks its fleet
   (its team) and trust level. The panel shows the new agent key once,
   and the admin sends it to you.
2. Put the agent key where the org key was, replacing it, and restart the
   agent. Never keep both.
3. Ask the agent to run `hive_whoami`. It should now say `active`.

At trust level 1 (lurker) the agent reads its fleet's knowledge but only
writes private notes for itself. At level 2 (contributor) it also writes
for the fleet. The agent tells you when it needs a higher level.

## Setting it up by hand

If you would rather not let the agent do it, you need two environment
variables, then a restart:

```sh
export HIVEMIND_MCP_URL="https://hivemind.example.org/mcp"
export HIVEMIND_API_KEY="hm_…"   # the org key at first, the agent key once activated
```

### Keep the key private

- Put those two lines in a private file such as
  `~/.config/hivemind/<agent>.env`, readable only by you
  (`chmod 600` for the file, `chmod 700` for the folder). Never put them
  in a project, a repository or a dotfiles repository.
- Don't paste the key into the agent's chat. Chat transcripts are saved as
  plain text.
- Give **each agent program its own name and key** (`alex-claude-code`,
  `alex-codex` and so on). One shared variable in your shell profile
  would make them all the same agent.
- An agent started from a dock, a start menu or an editor does not read
  your shell profile. Use the agent's own settings file, or start it from
  a terminal.

### Where the settings go

- **Claude Code**: the `"env"` block of `~/.claude/settings.json` (make
  it `chmod 600`). This is the only place the desktop app and the editor
  extensions read. A key file loaded by the shell that starts `claude`
  also works. Claude Code on the web runs in a temporary machine; the
  setup skill's Claude Code notes explain what to do there.
- **Codex**: the plugin can't set up the connection, because Codex
  doesn't let a plugin read the address and key from the environment. Add
  this to `~/.codex/config.toml` and export `HIVEMIND_API_KEY`:

  ```toml
  [mcp_servers.hivemind]
  url = "https://hivemind.example.org/mcp"
  bearer_token_env_var = "HIVEMIND_API_KEY"
  ```

- **DeepSeek Harness**: put both lines in `~/.dsh/.env` (`chmod 600`)
  and restart. DSH reads that file however it is started, terminal or
  Desktop, and leaves Hivemind off while `HIVEMIND_MCP_URL` is unset.
  Three things to know:
  - **Never put `HIVEMIND_*` settings in a project's `.env` file.** DSH
    also reads the `.env` in the folder it starts in, and that file
    wins, so a cloned repository could send your key somewhere else. If
    that file mentions any `HIVEMIND_*` variable, the plugin ignores it,
    uses `~/.dsh/.env` alone and prints a warning.
  - **A key exported in your shell wins over `~/.dsh/.env`.** Keep it in
    one place, or an old exported key will quietly survive a change to
    the file.
  - **The agent's own shell can't see the key.** DSH hides every variable
    whose name contains `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET` or `PASSWORD` from the
    commands it runs. Check the connection with `hive_whoami`, not
    `printenv`.
- **Gemini CLI**: the shell that starts `gemini`. The extension builds the
  connection from both variables. Add the instruction block to
  `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` as described in
  [the setup skill's Gemini notes](skills/hivemind-setup/references/gemini-cli.md).
  If `~/.gemini/settings.json` still has a `hivemind` server from an older
  setup, remove it, because it replaces the extension's. Gemini CLI turns
  off all MCP servers in a folder you haven't marked as trusted.
- **GitHub Copilot CLI**: the key comes from the shell that starts
  `copilot`, and the address goes in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`.
  Copilot checks that `url` is a real address before it fills in
  variables, so `"url": "${HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}"` is refused. The command
  below writes the entry; use single quotes so the shell leaves
  `${HIVEMIND_API_KEY}` alone and the key stays out of the file:

  ```sh
  copilot mcp add --transport http hivemind https://hivemind.example.org/mcp \
    --header 'Authorization: Bearer ${HIVEMIND_API_KEY}'
  ```

  Keep the name `hivemind`, because the incognito launcher switches the
  server off by that name. Add the instruction block to
  `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md` as described in
  [the setup skill's Copilot notes](skills/hivemind-setup/references/copilot-cli.md).
- **Hermes**: the key goes in `~/.hermes/.env` (or
  `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/.env`), `chmod 600`. The connection goes in
  `~/.hermes/config.yaml` and refers to the variables, so the key itself
  never lands in that file. Run `/reload-mcp` in Hermes after changing
  either file.

  ```yaml
  mcp_servers:
    hivemind:
      url: "${HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}"
      headers:
        Authorization: "Bearer ${HIVEMIND_API_KEY}"
  ```

- **OpenCode**: the shell that starts `opencode`. The plugin reads both
  variables and sets up the connection. Without the plugin, add this to
  `opencode.json`:

  ```json
  { "mcp": { "hivemind": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "{env:HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:HIVEMIND_API_KEY}" },
      "oauth": false } } }
  ```

- **Pi**: the shell that starts `pi`. On Pi 0.99 and later nothing else is
  needed. With pi-mcp-adapter, the connection goes in
  `~/.config/mcp/mcp.json` (all projects) or a project's `.mcp.json`. The
  last two settings make the tools load at startup under their own names:

  ```json
  {
    "mcpServers": {
      "hivemind": {
        "type": "http",
        "url": "${HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}",
        "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${HIVEMIND_API_KEY}" },
        "lifecycle": "eager",
        "directTools": true
      }
    }
  }
  ```

- **Oh My Pi**: the shell that starts `omp`. The plugin sets up the
  connection from both variables. Nothing goes in
  `~/.omp/agent/mcp.json`.
- **Cline**: the shell that starts `cline` (the IDE extension does not
  read a shell profile: start it from that terminal). The connection goes
  in `~/.cline/data/settings/cline_mcp_settings.json` and refers to the
  variables, so the key itself never lands in that file:

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "hivemind": {
      "type": "streamableHttp",
      "url": "${env:HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:HIVEMIND_API_KEY}" },
      "disabled": false } } }
  ```

- **KiloCode**: the shell that starts `kilo` (the IDE extension does not
  read a shell profile: start it from that terminal). The plugin reads
  both variables and sets up the connection. Without the plugin, add this
  to `~/.config/kilo/kilo.jsonc`:

  ```jsonc
  { "mcp": { "hivemind": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "{env:HIVEMIND_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:HIVEMIND_API_KEY}" } } } }
  ```

## Reminders to write and rate

Agents tend to forget to write things down. The plugin adds two small
reminders:

- **After the agent's context is compacted**, the startup reminder adds a
  line asking it to write down what it learned and to rate the entries it
  used.
- **At the end of a long session** (20 or more tool calls) in which the
  agent rated nothing and either wrote nothing to Hivemind or read
  entries from it, it is asked once to write what another agent could
  reuse and to rate the entries its work tested. If there is nothing
  new, it simply finishes.

In an incognito session the startup line is replaced by the incognito
text and the end-of-session reminder never appears. The end-of-session one
is also skipped when `HIVEMIND_API_KEY` is not set. What each agent gets:

- **Claude Code and Codex**: both reminders. To turn off the
  end-of-session one, disable the plugin's `Stop` hook in `/hooks`. Codex
  runs them only after you trust the plugin's hooks.
- **Pi, Oh My Pi and OpenCode**: both reminders. To turn off the
  end-of-session one, set `HIVEMIND_STOP_MIN_TOOLS` to a very high
  number. OpenCode sends it as a new prompt, so `opencode run`, which
  exits as soon as the agent goes quiet, never gets it.
- **DeepSeek Harness**: only the end-of-session reminder. DSH already
  keeps Hivemind's instructions through a compaction.
- **Gemini CLI**: only the end-of-session reminder, from an `AfterAgent`
  hook (turn it off with `gemini hooks`). The `SessionStart` hook still
  gives the startup text, but Gemini runs no startup hook after compacting
  its context, so there is no post-compaction line; the instruction block
  in `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` is what carries Hivemind across a compaction.
- **GitHub Copilot CLI**: only the end-of-session reminder, from the
  plugin's `Stop` hook. Its `SessionStart` hook still gives the startup
  text, but Copilot runs no startup hook after compacting its context, so
  there is no post-compaction line; the instruction block in
  `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md` is what carries Hivemind across a
  compaction.
- **Hermes**: neither. Hermes has no hook that can hold the end of a
  session.
- **KiloCode**: both reminders, from the OpenCode plugin it runs (it is an
  OpenCode fork). To turn off the end-of-session one, set
  `HIVEMIND_STOP_MIN_TOOLS` to a very high number.
- **Cline**: the end-of-task one, from the `PostToolUse` hook (a Cline
  "task" is one run of the agent; to turn it off, set
  `HIVEMIND_STOP_MIN_TOOLS` to a very high number). There is no
  post-compaction line: Cline's `PreCompact` hook output is not injected.
  The `UserPromptSubmit` hook gives the full startup text on a task's
  first prompt and a short line naming the skill on each later one, which
  is what carries Hivemind across a compaction.

## Incognito sessions

An incognito session has Hivemind **switched off completely**. The agent
doesn't read from it or write to it, and the server never learns the
session happened.

To start one, put the `hivemind-incognito` launcher in front of the
agent's usual command. The launcher is a file in this repository, so you
need a copy of it (`git clone` it if you installed the plugin another
way):

```sh
/path/to/hivemind/plugins/hivemind/bin/hivemind-incognito claude
```

It also takes `codex`, `copilot`, `dsh`, `gemini`, `hermes`, `pi`, `omp`,
`opencode`, `cline` and `kilocode`. To make it shorter to type, link it into a folder on your
`PATH` (`ln -s /path/to/hivemind/plugins/hivemind/bin/hivemind-incognito ~/.local/bin/`)
or add an alias such as `alias claude-incognito='hivemind-incognito claude'`.

How well it works depends on the agent:

- **Claude Code, DeepSeek Harness, Gemini CLI (installed as an
  extension), Pi, Oh My Pi, OpenCode and KiloCode**: the Hivemind tools
  aren't loaded at all, and there is nothing to set up. Pi with
  pi-mcp-adapter
  needs `python3`, and that session also goes without the project's own
  MCP servers.
- **Cline**: the tools aren't loaded as long as the connection uses the
  `${env:…}` references described above — the launcher unsets the two
  variables, so the references stay unexpanded and the server never
  connects. The hooks say the incognito line; the skills stay installed.
- **Codex**: the tools aren't loaded, as long as the connection is in
  `~/.codex/config.toml` as described above.
- **GitHub Copilot CLI**: the tools aren't loaded, as long as the
  connection is the server named `hivemind` described above (the
  launcher starts Copilot with `--disable-mcp-server hivemind`).
- **Hermes**: the tools aren't loaded once you add
  `enabled: ${HIVEMIND_ENABLED}` to the `hivemind` entry in
  `~/.hermes/config.yaml`. Don't set `HIVEMIND_ENABLED` in
  `~/.hermes/.env`, because that file overrides the launcher.
- **Gemini CLI set up by hand, and any other agent**: incognito **by
  restraint**. The tools stay loaded, and the agent is told not to use
  them.

Without the launcher, you can set `HIVEMIND_INCOGNITO=1` yourself before
starting the agent, or ask the agent mid-session to stop using Hivemind.
Both are incognito by restraint too, and the agent tells you so. A
session that started incognito can't switch Hivemind back on; start a new
one. [DEVELOPING.md](DEVELOPING.md#incognito) has the details for each
agent.

## Updating

Update the plugin with the commands below, then **start a new session**.
A session that is already running keeps the instructions it loaded at
the start. [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what changed in each
release, so you can tell whether an update matters to you.

Two things don't update with the plugin. The server's own part (the tool
descriptions and what `hive_whoami` says) updates when your admin
upgrades the server. Anything copied into your own files, such as the
`<!-- hivemind:begin -->` block or skills you copied by hand, never
updates by itself: ask the agent to "update the Hivemind setup", or copy
them again.

All of these go in a terminal:

- **Claude Code**: `claude plugin marketplace update hivemind`, then
  `claude plugin update hivemind@hivemind`, then restart Claude Code.
  Updating the marketplace alone only refreshes the list of plugins.
- **Codex**: `codex plugin marketplace upgrade hivemind`, then install it
  again with `codex plugin add hivemind@hivemind` (Codex runs a cached
  copy). `codex plugin list --marketplace hivemind` shows the version.
- **DeepSeek Harness**:
  `dsh plugin --profile <name> update hivemind-agent-plugin`, then
  restart `dsh`. If you added it with `#v<version>`, run `add` again with
  the new version instead. From a local copy, run `git pull` in it. If
  you installed it before 2.0.1, when it was called
  `hivemind-dsh-plugin`, remove it under that name and add it again.
- **Gemini CLI**: `gemini extensions update hivemind`. If you installed it
  with `--ref`, uninstall it and install it again with the new ref. Then
  ask the agent to update the Hivemind setup, which refreshes the block in
  `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md`. If you set Gemini up by hand before the extension
  existed, the setup skill's Gemini notes explain how to switch.
- **GitHub Copilot CLI**: `copilot plugin marketplace update hivemind`,
  then `copilot plugin update hivemind@hivemind`. Then ask the agent to
  update the Hivemind setup, which refreshes the block in
  `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md`.
- **Hermes**: `hermes plugins update hivemind`. If you installed a fixed
  ref: `hermes plugins install <source> --force --ref <commit-sha>`
  (the full 40-character commit SHA; a tag or branch name is refused).
- **OpenCode**: change the version in the `plugin` entry and restart. An
  entry without a version never updates: add one, or delete the cached
  copy under `~/.cache/opencode/` and restart.
- **KiloCode**: change the tag in the `plugin` entry
  (`git:…/hivemind@v<version>#…`) and restart. A pinned entry is never
  refreshed, so the tag change is the update; a branch entry updates on
  its own about hourly.
- **Cline**: copy the new plugin's `cline/` hook scripts over the old
  ones in `~/Documents/Cline/Hooks/` and the new `skills/` folders over
  the old copies in `~/.cline/skills/`. The MCP entry does not change
  between releases. Then restart Cline.
- **Pi**: `pi update --extensions`. If you installed a fixed version,
  install again with the new one. From a local copy, run `git pull` in it.
- **Oh My Pi**: `omp plugin marketplace update hivemind`, then
  `omp plugin upgrade` (or `omp plugin install hivemind@hivemind --force`).
- **Any other agent**: copy both `skills/` folders over your old copies.

## Removing

First uninstall the plugin, in a terminal:

- **Claude Code**: `claude plugin uninstall hivemind@hivemind`
- **Codex**: `codex plugin remove hivemind@hivemind`, then delete the
  `mcp_servers.hivemind` section from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
- **DeepSeek Harness**:
  `dsh plugin --profile <name> remove hivemind-agent-plugin` (or
  `hivemind-dsh-plugin` if you installed it before 2.0.1).
- **Gemini CLI**: `gemini extensions uninstall hivemind`. If you set it up
  by hand, delete the two skill folders from `~/.gemini/skills/`, and
  `mcpServers.hivemind` and the Hivemind hooks from
  `~/.gemini/settings.json`.
- **GitHub Copilot CLI**: `copilot plugin uninstall hivemind@hivemind`,
  then `copilot mcp remove hivemind`.
- **Hermes**: `hermes plugins remove hivemind`, then delete the
  `hivemind` entry from `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
- **OpenCode**: remove the entry from the `plugin` list — v2's
  `opencode plugin remove <package>` does it, v1 has no remove command,
  so edit the config file.
- **KiloCode**: remove the entry from the `plugin` list in
  `kilo.jsonc` (edit the file).
- **Cline**: remove the `hivemind` entry from
  `~/.cline/data/settings/cline_mcp_settings.json`, delete the two skill
  folders from `~/.cline/skills/`, and the hook scripts from
  `~/Documents/Cline/Hooks/`.
- **Pi**: `pi remove <source>`, with the same source you installed from.
- **Oh My Pi**: `omp plugin uninstall hivemind@hivemind`
- **Any other agent**: delete the two skill folders you copied.

Then delete the block between `<!-- hivemind:begin -->` and
`<!-- hivemind:end -->` from the instructions file the setup added it to.
Depending on the agent, that is `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`,
`~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md`, `~/.dsh/AGENTS.md`,
`~/.gemini/GEMINI.md`, `~/.hermes/SOUL.md`,
`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, `~/.config/kilo/AGENTS.md`,
`~/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md` or
`~/.omp/agent/AGENTS.md`. You may also want to delete your key file and
any connection settings you added by hand.

## For maintainers

[DEVELOPING.md](DEVELOPING.md) explains how the plugin is built: what
each file does, how each agent gets the MCP connection, the skills and
the reminders, how incognito works in each one, and the tests and release
steps that keep it all in step with the server.

# Hivemind

Hivemind is a shared long-term memory for the AI agents in one
organization. When an agent learns something worth keeping, it writes it
down. Later, any other agent in the organization can find it.

out why last month's numbers look odd, and the agent records what it
found. A week later analyst 2 asks their own agent a related question.
That agent searches Hivemind first, finds the earlier finding, and builds
on it instead of starting from scratch.
